title: Half of America No Longer Trusts the CDC. For South Asians Who Grew Up Trusting Public Health, the Ground Just Shifted.
excerpt: A Harvard poll finds trust in the CDC has cratered from 77 to 50 per cent in a single year. For a diaspora that built its American life around institutional credibility, the fallout is personal.
body:
For most first-generation Indian Americans, the CDC was not just a government acronym. It was the institution you cited when your mother-in-law questioned why you were vaccinating the baby on an American schedule instead of the Indian one. It was the website you checked before booking tickets to Chennai during dengue season. It was the authority you trusted more than WhatsApp forwards, more than aunties, more than YouTube naturopaths.

That authority just lost half the country.

## The Numbers Are Stark

A new poll from Harvard University's T.H. Chan School of Public Health and the de Beaumont Foundation, conducted among roughly 2,200 adults between March and April 2026, found that just 50 per cent of Americans now trust health recommendations from the CDC. In spring 2025, that number was 77 per cent. The collapse is one of the steepest recorded for any federal institution in a single year.

The partisan split is dramatic. Among Democrats, trust in the CDC dropped from 92 per cent to 34 per cent. Among Independents, it fell from 77 per cent to 47 per cent. Republicans, meanwhile, moved in the opposite direction — from 63 per cent to 67 per cent — reflecting broad approval of the Trump administration's overhaul of federal health agencies under Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.

The erosion extends beyond the CDC. Only 53 per cent of respondents said they trust the Food and Drug Administration and the National Institutes of Health to improve health. And roughly 60 per cent of all adults — across party lines — said the government has gone too far in cutting research funding.

## What Changed in One Year

Since the last poll was conducted, the administration has fired longtime vaccine scientists, pushed out senior CDC leadership, stopped coordinating with the World Health Organization, sought to reduce the number of recommended childhood vaccines, and altered the US food pyramid to encourage more red meat. Courts have challenged several of these actions.

Eighty-six per cent of Democrats disapprove. Eighty per cent of Republicans approve. The CDC's guidance has become something Americans evaluate through a political lens, not a scientific one.

There is one surviving pocket of trust: people still overwhelmingly trust their own doctors, nurses, and pharmacists, as well as independent health organisations like the American Heart Association and American Cancer Society. Over 80 per cent of respondents expressed confidence in these groups. The erosion is institutional, not interpersonal.

## The Diaspora's Specific Dilemma

For South Asians in America, this collapse lands differently than it does for most Americans. Many first-generation immigrants arrived from a country where public health infrastructure — despite its gaps — carries real weight. AIIMS, ICMR, the national immunisation programme: these are institutions people grow up trusting, even when they complain about the system. Moving to America meant moving into a country where the equivalent institutions were, if anything, even more credible.

Now the institution that told you when your child needed the MMR, what to do during COVID, and whether it was safe to travel during flu season is being described by its own government as bloated, biased, and in need of radical restructuring.

The practical consequences are immediate. Paediatricians across the country report that parents are now asking which vaccines are "really necessary" and which were "political." Public health officials say this kind of selective scepticism — born not from anti-vaccine ideology but from institutional distrust — is harder to counter than outright denialism.

For NRI families who split time between India and America, the confusion compounds. India's immunisation schedule does not match the American one. The CDC was the tiebreaker. Without it, parents are left comparing WhatsApp groups, competing national guidelines, and their own instincts — a situation that benefits no one except the virus.

## What Survives

The poll offers one thread of hope. Trust in local public health agencies remains high: 70 per cent of respondents trust their local health department, and 66 per cent trust their state-level agencies. This suggests that public health credibility is fracturing, not disappearing. It is moving from the federal to the local, from the institutional to the personal.

For the Indian American community — where the family doctor still occupies a position of near-religious authority — this shift may be manageable. The paediatrician you have known for a decade still matters more than any CDC press release. But the paediatrician, until now, was translating CDC guidance into family-level decisions. When the source code is corrupted, the downstream effects are unpredictable.

The question is no longer whether Americans trust the CDC. It is what fills the vacuum when they do not. For a diaspora that crossed oceans partly because it believed in the reliability of American institutions, the answer matters more than most.
